# Blueprint Design & Management

You manage Facets blueprints via `raptor` commands in Bash.

Raptor operates on **projects** containing **resources** deployed across **environments**.
Resources are infrastructure components defined by KIND/FLAVOR/VERSION (e.g., `service/aws/1.0`).
Resources reference each other via `${type.name.out.field}` expressions.

**Conventions:**
- Resource identifier: `KIND/NAME` (e.g., `service/api`, `postgres/main-db`)
- Module identifier: `KIND/FLAVOR/VERSION` (e.g., `service/aws/1.0`)
- Prefer long flags: `--project`, `--environment`
- Use `-o json` for programmatic parsing
- All commands support: `-o table` (default), `-o wide`, `-o json`, `-o yaml`

> **Read stderr as well as stdout.** raptor splits its output across both
> streams, and the warnings are the half that changes what the result means:
> "that `--unset` key isn't present", "`--overwrite` is discarding these keys",
> "no schema available, applying without validation", "the blueprint spec above
> is NOT what runs there". Progress chatter (`🔍 Fetching … schema`) goes to
> **stdout**, so capturing stdout alone gets you the noise and drops the
> warnings. When you run a raptor command, capture `2>&1` or read both.

> **The `spec.` prefix differs between the two apply commands.** This is silent
> when you get it wrong — no error, the command reports success, nothing happens.
> ```bash
> raptor apply resource ... --set replicas=3        # blueprint: NO prefix
> raptor apply override  ... --set spec.replicas=3  # override:  prefix REQUIRED
> ```
> On an override, `--set disabled=false` writes `spec.disabled` — a meaningless
> spec field — instead of the top-level `disabled` pin. Use `--enabled`. The same
> applies to `flavor`, `version` and `advanced.inherit_from_base`: they are
> top-level fields, `--set`/`--unset` cannot reach them, and the tool for
> removing them is `raptor delete override --path`.

## 1. Discover

Explore existing state before making changes.

```bash
raptor get projects
raptor get resources -p PROJECT
raptor get resources KIND/NAME -p PROJECT            # Blueprint spec for one resource
raptor get environments -p PROJECT
raptor get variables -p PROJECT
raptor get variable VARNAME -p PROJECT
raptor get variable-usages VARNAME -p PROJECT        # which resources reference it

# What changed and when — blueprint / override / artifact streams for one resource
raptor get resources KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV --history
raptor get resources KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV --history --diff blueprint
raptor get resources KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV --history --version override/v2 -o json
```

`--history` requires `-e` (resource history is cluster-scoped). `--diff` takes a
stream (`blueprint`, `override` or `artifact`), optionally with a range —
`--diff blueprint/v3..v5`. Cross-stream ranges are rejected. Note the asymmetry
with `get overrides --history --diff`, where a bare `--diff` is allowed and
means previous-vs-latest.

> **The blueprint spec is NOT per-environment truth.** `raptor get resources KIND/NAME -p PROJECT`
> (no `-e`) returns the project-level *base* spec. A resource can be overridden per
> environment — including being **disabled** in some environments while the base shows
> it enabled. When a resource has overrides, this command prints a hint **to stderr**
> naming which environments differ (config vs disabled) — always read it. **Never assume
> the base spec is what actually runs.** Before reasoning about, debugging, or editing a
> resource's behavior in a specific environment, confirm the effective config:
> ```bash
> raptor get resources KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV    # blueprint + overrides + effective (merged)
> raptor get overrides  KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV    # just the override delta for that env
> ```

**Reading the env-scoped response.** `-o json`/`-o yaml` returns the three
sections plus two fields that tell you which is which — read them before the
sections themselves:

| field | what it gives you |
|---|---|
| `_about` | one line per section, naming the environment: which is the shared base, which are this env's pins, and which is what actually runs |
| `pinnedKeys` | the dotted paths this environment overrides. **These are the keys that will ignore future blueprint edits.** Absent when nothing is pinned. |

`.effective` is the answer to "what runs in ENV". `.blueprint` is the
project-wide base and answers nothing about any single environment.

## 2. Environments & Accounts

Set up environments and link cloud accounts.

```bash
# Create and launch an environment
raptor create environment NAME -p PROJECT --launch -w
raptor create environment NAME -p PROJECT --release-stream STREAM --launch -w

# Launch an existing environment
raptor launch environment NAME -p PROJECT -w

# NOTE: Launch bootstraps infrastructure with resources disabled.
# Follow with a release to deploy resources:
# raptor create release -p PROJECT -e NAME -w

# Destroy environment infrastructure (terraform destroy)
raptor destroy environment NAME -p PROJECT --yes -w

# Delete environment record (after destroy)
raptor delete environment NAME -p PROJECT --yes

# Link cloud accounts (aws, gcp, azure, kubernetes)
raptor create account --provider aws --name NAME -w
raptor create account --provider gcp --name NAME -w
```

The link command prints a script to run in a terminal authenticated with the cloud provider CLI.

## 3. Describe

Understand module schemas, available expressions, and dependencies before building.

**Module details** (always do this before creating a resource):
```bash
raptor describe module KIND/FLAVOR/VERSION                  # Inputs, outputs, spec schema
raptor describe module KIND/FLAVOR/VERSION --for-override   # Override-eligible fields only
raptor describe module KIND/FLAVOR/VERSION --schema         # Raw JSON Schema
```

**Expressions** (valid `${}` paths for wiring resources):
```bash
raptor describe expressions -p PROJECT                              # All paths
raptor describe expressions -p PROJECT KIND/NAME                    # From specific resource
raptor describe expressions -p PROJECT --kind KIND                  # Filter by kind
raptor describe expressions -p PROJECT --include KIND/FLAVOR/VER:NAME  # Include pending resource
```

**Impact analysis** (understand dependency graph):
```bash
raptor impact KIND/NAME -p PROJECT              # Downstream: what breaks if this changes
raptor impact KIND/NAME -p PROJECT --reverse    # Upstream: what this depends on
```

## 4. Apply Resources

Create or update resources using imperative CLI flags.

```bash
raptor apply resource KIND/FLAVOR/VERSION -p PROJECT -n NAME [flags]
```

> **HARD RULE — always prefer `--set` over `--spec`.** `--set KEY=VALUE` merges
> into the existing resource: fields you don't mention are preserved. `--spec`
> and `--spec-file` REPLACE the entire spec section, silently dropping every
> field not present in the payload. Only use `--spec`/`--spec-file` if the user
> has explicitly asked to replace the entire spec from scratch. When you do use
> them, raptor will prompt to confirm the destructive replace; pass `--yes` to
> proceed non-interactively after you've confirmed with the user. Tracked in
> raptor#141.

**Flags:**
- `--set KEY=VALUE` — set spec field, dot-notation, merges (repeatable) — **default tool for any spec change**
- `--unset KEY` — remove spec field (repeatable)
- `--input INPUT_NAME=KIND/RESOURCE[/OUTPUT]` — wire input (repeatable)
- `--unset-input INPUT_NAME` — remove input (repeatable)
- `--spec '{"key":"val"}'` — **destructive**: full replace of spec; only use when explicitly replacing the entire spec
- `--spec-file spec.yaml` — **destructive**: full replace from file; same caveat as `--spec`
- `--yes` / `-y` — skip the destructive-replace confirmation prompt
- `--disabled` — mark resource disabled in the blueprint (excluded from releases in all envs)
- `--enabled` — re-enable a resource (sets disabled=false); use to reverse a previous `--disabled`
- `--dry-run` — validate and print without applying
- `--save-to FILE` — save resource YAML to file

**Examples:**
```bash
# Create a new resource with inputs and spec
raptor apply resource service/aws/1.0 -p myproject -n my-api \
  --input cloud_account=cloud_account/aws \
  --set type=application \
  --set runtime.size.cpu=500m \
  --set runtime.size.memory=512Mi

# Update an existing resource (merges with current)
raptor apply resource service/aws/1.0 -p myproject -n my-api \
  --set runtime.size.memory=1Gi

# Validate without applying
raptor apply resource service/aws/1.0 -p myproject -n my-api \
  --set type=application --dry-run
```

### Convert a resource to a mustache template

Turn an existing JSON resource into a `.mustache` template (the UI's "Convert to
Mustache"): raptor re-sends the resource's current content as `rawContent`, and
the server replaces the `.json` file with a `.mustache` one in a single commit.
Content is unchanged — only the format. One-directional (no mustache→JSON).

```bash
raptor convert resource service/api -p PROJECT --to-mustache        # prompts
raptor convert resource service/api -p PROJECT --to-mustache -y -m "convert"
```

Errors if already mustache; a headless run without `-y` refuses (never a silent
no-op). After converting, edit the `.mustache` and re-apply with `apply -f
resource.mustache`.

### Template inputs (two levels — mind the scope)

- **Template input TYPE = blueprint level** (the schema/field list, one per
  project; a `template_input_type` blueprint resource — NO `-e`):
  ```bash
  raptor get template-input-types -p PROJECT
  raptor apply template-input-type -f type.json -p PROJECT [--name NAME]   # create/update
  raptor delete template-input-type NAME -p PROJECT [-y]                   # delete (blueprint)
  ```
- **Template input ITEMS = environment level** (per-cluster values of a type;
  require `-e`):
  ```bash
  raptor get template-inputs -p PROJECT -e ENV
  raptor create template-input TYPE/UID -p PROJECT -e ENV --field K=V ...
  raptor set   template-input TYPE/UID -p PROJECT -e ENV --field K=V
  raptor delete template-input TYPE/UID [TYPE/UID...] -p PROJECT -e ENV [-y]
  ```

Deleting a TYPE removes the blueprint definition only; its per-environment ITEMS
are separate records — delete those first if you want them gone. All deletes are
TTY-aware: a headless run without `-y` refuses instead of silently cancelling.

## 5. Apply Overrides

Per-environment customization (replicas, memory, domains). Merges by default.

```bash
raptor apply override KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV [flags]
```

> **HARD RULE — always prefer `--set` over `--spec`.** `--set KEY=VALUE` merges
> into the existing override: previously-set fields you don't mention are
> preserved. `--spec` and `--spec-file` REPLACE the entire override spec
> section, silently dropping every existing override field not present in the
> payload (this caused a production outage on `niyo-forex / prod-niyo-forex /
> service/customer-master` — a `--spec` invocation wiped `health_check` and
> other overrides). Only use `--spec`/`--spec-file` if the user has explicitly
> asked to replace the entire override spec. When you do, raptor will prompt
> to confirm the destructive replace; pass `--yes` only after confirming with
> the user. Tracked in raptor#141.

**Flags:**
- `--set KEY=VALUE` — set override field, dot-notation, merges (repeatable) — **default tool for any override change**
- `--unset KEY` — remove override field (repeatable). **Also the way to release a pin:** removing a key whose value already equals the blueprint value is not a no-op — the effective config is unchanged, but the key leaves the override document so future blueprint edits reach this environment again. If the key isn't present, the command warns on stderr and exits 0, so re-running a removal that already landed is safe. Only reaches spec fields — for `disabled`/`flavor`/`version` use `delete override --path`
- `--spec '{"key":"val"}'` — **destructive**: full replace of override spec; only use when explicitly replacing the whole spec
- `--spec-file FILE` — **destructive**: full replace from file; same caveat as `--spec`
- `--yes` / `-y` — skip the destructive-replace confirmation prompt
- `--overwrite` — nuke: discard all existing overrides, rebuild from this invocation. Keys you don't restate are **lost**, including `disabled`/`flavor`/`version` pins; the command names them on **stderr** before applying — read it. **Cannot be combined with `--unset`** (rejected before any network call): the rebuild starts from an empty document, so there'd be nothing to remove. To drop one key use `--unset` alone; to clear the override entirely use `delete override`
- `--disabled` — disable resource in this environment only
- `--enabled` — re-enable resource in this environment (sets disabled=false in the override; reverses `--disabled`). This is the way to turn ON a base-disabled resource in one env — do NOT try `--set disabled=false` (writes `spec.disabled`, which does nothing)
- `--dry-run` — print without applying
- `-m "message"` — changelog message

**Examples:**
```bash
# Scale up for production
raptor apply override service/api -p myproject -e prod \
  --set spec.replicas=10 --set spec.runtime.size.memory=4Gi

# Remove a field
raptor apply override service/api -p myproject -e prod --unset spec.runtime.cpu_limit

# Release a pin whose value already matches the blueprint. Nothing running
# changes; the key stops ignoring future blueprint edits in this environment.
raptor apply override redis/cache -p myproject -e prod \
  --unset spec.sizing.snapshot_window --yes

# Disable in staging
raptor apply override service/api -p myproject -e staging --disabled

# Re-enable in staging (also how you turn ON a base-disabled resource in one env)
raptor apply override service/api -p myproject -e staging --enabled
```

**Delete all overrides** (revert to blueprint; `-e` is repeatable for several envs):
```bash
raptor delete override KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV
```

**Copy one environment's configuration onto another** — this copies **override
documents**, so the target's pins become the source's pins. Scope it with
`--include`/`--exclude` (e.g. `OVERRIDES`, `VARIABLES_SECRETS`, `ARTIFACTS`):
```bash
raptor copy config -p PROJECT --from dev --to staging
raptor copy config -p PROJECT --from dev --to staging --exclude OVERRIDES
```

**Delete specific override FIELDS across environments** — one server call per
resource covering every listed env (the UI's "Reset Selected"):
```bash
raptor delete override service/api -p PROJECT -e dev -e prod --path spec.replicas --path spec.cpu
```

### Bulk state operations (many resources per call)

Selectors work on both commands below: positional `KIND/NAME...`, `--type KIND`
(every resource of a kind), `--resources-file FILE` (newline-delimited
`KIND/NAME`, `#` comments allowed). Every bulk run shows a preview and a
`--yes`-gated confirm; `--dry-run` previews without applying; a headless run
without `--yes` refuses with a clear error instead of silently cancelling.

```bash
# ENVIRONMENT level — edits override docs, one batched PUT per state group
raptor apply override -p PROJECT -e ENV --disabled service/a service/b
raptor apply override -p PROJECT -e ENV --inherit --type pubsub          # mark inheritable
raptor apply override -p PROJECT -e ENV --disabled --inherit service/a   # combo: toggle then inherit

# BLUEPRINT level — edits resource files, ONE git commit per call, all envs synced
raptor apply resource -p PROJECT --disabled service/a service/b -m "why"
raptor apply resource -p PROJECT --inherit --resources-file list.txt

# Attach many resources to a resource group in ONE call (detach stays per-resource)
raptor attach resource service/a service/b --group GROUP -p PROJECT
```

- Toggle previews resolve and list the child resources the server will also
  toggle; inherit changes touch only the listed resources (no child expansion).
- `--inherit` / `--no-inherit` set `advanced.inherit_from_base` true/false.
- Blueprint bulk state takes `KIND/NAME` targets (one slash) — never mix with
  the `KIND/FLAVOR/VERSION` envelope form. Avoid mustache-templated resources
  as blueprint-level targets; environment level is unaffected by mustache-ness.
- Already-in-state targets are harmless no-ops (server upserts idempotently).
- `delete resource-group` accepts the group NAME or its ID.

### Override history & rollback

Every override change is versioned. Inspect the history and roll back to a
previous revision — use these whenever the user asks to "rollback", "revert",
"restore", or "undo" an override change:

```bash
# List revisions (version, date, author, changelog, change summary)
raptor get overrides KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV --history

# Diff two revisions (defaults to previous vs latest when bare --diff)
raptor get overrides KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV --history --diff v3..v5

# Dump one revision's full content
raptor get overrides KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV --history --version 3 -o json

# Roll back to the previous revision (undo the last override change)
raptor rollback override KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV

# Roll back to a specific revision from --history
raptor rollback override KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV --version 3

# Preview the rollback diff without applying; --yes for non-interactive
raptor rollback override KIND/NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV --version 3 --dry-run
```

`rollback override` shows the effective-config diff and asks for confirmation
before mutating (`--yes` skips the prompt — non-interactive runs need it). The
rollback is recorded as a **new** revision whose content equals the target, so
history is never rewound and a rollback can itself be rolled back. It is
audited as an override version rollback. The environment picks up the restored
configuration on its next release — create one to deploy it.

## 6. Plan & Validate

Pre-flight validation before deploying. Checks expressions, cycles, input wiring, and optionally runs terraform plan.

```bash
# Local validation only (fast)
raptor plan -p PROJECT -e ENV --skip-server-plan

# Full plan with terraform
raptor plan -p PROJECT -e ENV

# Targeted plan
raptor plan -p PROJECT -e ENV --target KIND/NAME --target KIND/NAME
```

**Flags:**
- `--skip-server-plan` — local validation only
- `--target KIND/NAME` — scope to specific resources (repeatable)
- `--force` — plan even if no changes
- `--allow-destroy` — allow resource destruction
- `-m "message"` — plan comment

## 7. Deploy

Trigger releases (Terraform apply).

```bash
raptor create release -p PROJECT -e ENV [flags]
```

**Flags:**
- `--plan` — dry-run plan only, no apply
- `--target KIND/NAME` — selective release (repeatable)
- `-w` — wait and tail logs
- `--force` — force even if no changes
- `--allow-destroy` — allow destruction
- `--with-refresh` — refresh Terraform state first
- `-m "message"` — changelog

**Examples:**
```bash
raptor create release -p myproject -e dev -w                          # Full release
raptor create release -p myproject -e dev --plan -w                   # Plan only
raptor create release -p myproject -e dev --target service/api -w     # Selective
```

## 7a. Pre-release Approval Hook

Gate a project's releases behind manual approval. The hook is a script stored in
the blueprint and run before each release; its **exit code** decides the outcome:
- `exit 0` — proceed
- `exit 2` — require approval (the release parks in PENDING_APPROVAL)
- any other non-zero — the release fails

You author the script; the control plane stores it verbatim at
`pre_release_hooks/pre_release_hook.py` (Python) or `pre_release_hook.sh` (Shell).
At run time the hook receives the path to a `release_changes.json` as its first
argument (fields: `environmentName`, `releaseStream`, `triggeredBy`, and
`resources[]` — each with `resourceType`, `resourceName`, `resourcePath`,
`changeType`). **A hook must only ever exit 0 or 2** — an unhandled error that
exits 1 fails the release instead of gating it, so wrap logic defensively and exit
deliberately.

The commands take `--type` to select the hook kind (default `pre-release`, the
only type today). The language is Python by default — use `--language python|shell`,
or just point `--script-file` at a `.sh`/`.py` file and it's inferred. Only one hook
exists per project — switching language replaces the other file.

```bash
# Show the current hook (prints language + path)
raptor get hook --type pre-release -p PROJECT

# Install/replace — language inferred from the file extension
raptor apply hook --type pre-release -p PROJECT --script-file ./pre_release_hook.py   # Python
raptor apply hook --type pre-release -p PROJECT --script-file ./pre_release_hook.sh   # Shell

# Inline body with explicit language
raptor apply hook --type pre-release -p PROJECT --language shell --script 'exit 0'

# Remove the hook (destructive). Without --yes the CLI prompts for
# interactive confirmation — the safe default. Only add --yes after the
# user has explicitly confirmed the removal.
raptor delete hook --type pre-release -p PROJECT
raptor delete hook --type pre-release -p PROJECT --yes   # skips the prompt; use only post-confirmation
```

**Acting on a release the hook parked in PENDING_APPROVAL.** Installing the gate
is only half of it — these are how it gets opened or closed:

```bash
raptor approve release RELEASE_ID -p PROJECT -e ENV
raptor reject  release RELEASE_ID -p PROJECT -e ENV
raptor abort   release RELEASE_ID -p PROJECT -e ENV   # emergency stop, any state
```

Get the RELEASE_ID from `raptor get releases -p PROJECT -e ENV`.

**Example hook — require approval for specific environments:**
```python
import json, sys
GATED_ENVIRONMENTS = ["prod", "gcp-infra-dev"]
try:
    with open(sys.argv[1]) as f:
        release = json.load(f)
    if release.get("environmentName") in GATED_ENVIRONMENTS:
        sys.exit(2)   # require approval
    sys.exit(0)       # proceed
except SystemExit:
    raise
except Exception:
    sys.exit(0)       # fail-open: never hard-fail a release on a hook glitch
```

**Same gate as a shell hook:**
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
env=$(jq -r '.environmentName' "$1")
case "$env" in
  prod|gcp-infra-dev) exit 2 ;;   # require approval
  *) exit 0 ;;                     # proceed
esac
```

## 8. Custom Releases (Terraform State Operations)

Custom releases run terraform commands against a resource's state instead of the standard plan/apply cycle. Use for state inspection and state surgery.

**This is an advanced operation. Incorrect state manipulation can orphan cloud resources or destroy infrastructure.**

```bash
# List all resources in state for a resource
terraform state list

# Inspect a specific resource's state
terraform state show module.application.<resource_address>

# Remove a resource from state (DANGEROUS — only if the cloud resource
# is already deleted or you intentionally want to orphan it)
terraform state rm module.application.<resource_address>
```

Trigger these with `raptor create custom-release` — `-c` is repeatable and runs
the commands in order:

```bash
raptor create custom-release -p PROJECT -e ENV -c "terraform state list"
raptor create custom-release -p PROJECT -e ENV -c "terraform state show module.application.ADDRESS"
raptor create custom-release -p PROJECT -e ENV -c "terraform state rm module.application.ADDRESS" --allow-destroy
raptor create custom-release -p PROJECT -e ENV -c "echo start" -c "terraform version" -m "why"
```

`--allow-destroy` is required for anything destructive — never pass it unless
the user has explicitly asked for that operation.

**Safety rules:**
- Always `terraform state list` or `terraform state show` first — understand what you're operating on
- Never `terraform state rm` unless you are certain the cloud resource is already deleted or you accept orphaning it
- Custom releases run in the same execution environment as regular releases — same providers, same state backend
- Review the release logs afterward to confirm the operation succeeded

## 9. Monitor

Check deployment results and resource state.

```bash
raptor logs release -p PROJECT -e ENV RELEASE_ID --stream # View logs (--stream tees content to stdout; without it only the temp-file path is printed)
raptor logs release -p PROJECT -e ENV -f RELEASE_ID       # Stream/follow logs
raptor get resource-outputs -p PROJECT -e ENV KIND/NAME   # Runtime outputs
raptor get resource-status -p PROJECT -e ENV KIND/NAME    # Deployment status
raptor get releases -p PROJECT -e ENV                     # find a RELEASE_ID
raptor debug release RELEASE_ID "ls -la"                  # run a command inside the release pod
```

`debug release` is the escalation when logs aren't enough — it executes your
command in the release's own execution environment.

## 10. Variables & Secrets

Manage project-level configuration values.

```bash
raptor get variables -p PROJECT
raptor get variable VARNAME -p PROJECT
raptor get variable-usages VARNAME -p PROJECT   # the resources referencing one name
raptor get variable-usages -p PROJECT           # every name, with what nothing uses
raptor create variable VARNAME -p PROJECT --default "VALUE"
raptor create variable SECRETNAME -p PROJECT --secret --env-values ENV=secret
raptor set variable VARNAME -p PROJECT --value "NEW_VALUE"
raptor set variable SECRETNAME -p PROJECT --env-values ENV=newsecret
raptor delete variable VARNAME -p PROJECT
```

Secrets never have a stack-level default value (`--default`/`--value` are
variables-only). Secret values are set per environment via `--env-values` —
even if the value should be the same in every environment, set it for each
environment separately.

Reference in specs: `${blueprint.self.variables.NAME}`, `${blueprint.self.secrets.NAME}`

`variable-usages` is the reverse lookup, and covers both nouns — check it before
deleting a name, since `delete variable` refuses one that is still referenced. A
`blueprint` row reaches every environment the resource deploys to; an `env/NAME`
row is a resource that exists only there.

## 11. Auth

```bash
raptor whoami
raptor auth can-i PERMISSION -p PROJECT [-e ENV]
```

## 12. Resource Inheritance

Resource inheritance allows a dependent environment to reference a resource from a base environment instead of deploying its own copy. This is useful for sharing infrastructure (e.g., a database or cloud account) across environments or even across projects.

### Same-Project Inheritance

When environments in the same project share a base–dependent relationship, a dependent environment can inherit a resource from the base environment. Set `advanced.inherit_from_base: true` in the resource JSON/YAML.

**Steps:**
1. Identify the resource to inherit (e.g., `postgres/main-db`)
2. Fetch the existing resource and add the `advanced` block
3. Apply the updated resource

```bash
# 1. Get the current resource as JSON
raptor get resources -p PROJECT -o json | jq '.[] | select(.resourceType=="KIND" and .resourceName=="NAME")'

# 2. Create or update the resource file with advanced.inherit_from_base
# The resource YAML should look like:
```

```yaml
kind: postgres
flavor: rds
version: "0.2"
disabled: false
metadata:
  name: main-db
advanced:
  inherit_from_base: true
spec:
  # ... existing spec ...
```

```bash
# 3. Apply the resource
raptor apply -f resource.yaml -p PROJECT

# 4. Release in the dependent environment — it will reference the base environment's resource
raptor create release -p PROJECT -e DEPENDENT_ENV -w
```

The dependent environment will **not** deploy its own copy of this resource. Instead, it will use the outputs (connection strings, endpoints, etc.) from the base environment's deployed resource.

### Cross-Project Inheritance

To share a resource across two different Facets projects, the resource with the **same name** must exist in both projects with `advanced.inherit_from_base: true`.

**Steps:**
1. Ensure the resource exists in the **base project** (the project that actually deploys the resource)
2. Add the same resource (same `kind`, `metadata.name`) in the **dependent project** with `advanced.inherit_from_base: true`
3. Apply in both projects

The resource YAML is **identical to the same-project form above** — the only
requirement is that the same `kind` AND `metadata.name` exist in both projects,
each carrying `advanced.inherit_from_base: true`.

```bash
raptor apply -f shared-db.yaml -p BASE_PROJECT        # the project that deploys it
raptor apply -f shared-db.yaml -p DEPENDENT_PROJECT   # same file, same resource name
```

### Inheritance Rules

- The `advanced.inherit_from_base` flag is set at the **blueprint level** (not per-environment)
- The resource `metadata.name` must match exactly across projects for cross-project inheritance
- The dependent environment skips deployment of the inherited resource and references outputs from the base
- Use `raptor get resource-outputs` to verify the inherited resource outputs are available in the dependent environment
- Inheritance works with any resource type (services, databases, cloud accounts, etc.)

## Key Principles

1. Always `describe module` before creating resources — never guess structure
2. Always `describe expressions` for valid `${}` references
3. Always `plan` before `create release`
4. Use `--dry-run` on apply commands to validate first
5. Use `impact` before modifying resources with dependents
6. Keep overrides minimal — base config should work broadly
7. The blueprint spec (`get resources KIND/NAME` without `-e`) is the base, not per-env truth — heed the stderr override hint and verify effective config with `-e ENV` before trusting it

## Sensitive Values in Raptor Commands — NEVER Put Secrets in the Chat

**CRITICAL RULE: NEVER ask the user to type a sensitive value (password, token, API
key, secret) in the chat.** Typing it in chat means the LLM sees it — it will be stored
in conversation history and logs. This is forbidden regardless of which tool you use to
ask (AskUserQuestion, chat message, follow-up question — all forbidden for secrets).

**Mandatory workflow — no exceptions:**

You run under the user's own shell — there is no vault or modal here. Keep the secret
out of the chat by having the user put it in an environment variable in their terminal,
then reference the *variable* (never the value) in raptor commands:

```bash
# 1. The user runs this in their own terminal. `read -rs` reads at a silent prompt,
#    so the value is never pasted into the chat and never reaches the LLM or transcript:
read -rs MY_DB_PASS; export MY_DB_PASS

# 2. Reference the env var in the raptor command. The user's shell expands "$MY_DB_PASS"
#    locally — the literal value never appears in what you (the LLM) emit or log.
#    Secrets never take a stack-level --value — set them per environment:
raptor create variable MY_DB_PASS -p myproject --secret --env-values prod="$MY_DB_PASS"
```

If a value should not even transit an env var, ask the user to run the single sensitive
raptor command themselves and paste back only the (non-sensitive) result.

**If the user offers to type the value in chat, redirect them:**
"Please don't paste it in chat — export it in your shell (`read -rs MY_DB_PASS; export
MY_DB_PASS`) and I'll reference `$MY_DB_PASS`, so the value never enters our conversation."

The `--secret` flag marks the variable as sensitive in the Facets Control Plane
(masked in UI, not returned in plain-text API responses).
